conversation.content: Well  [Redacted] and the job title is not as important as it may sound but anyway. conversation.speaker: AZ

conversation.content: What do you see as the future of the delta  20 years from now, or even 50 years from now?

conversation.speaker: JH
conversation.content: Those are difficult questions. My perspective is different than most people you'll talk to just because of our unique situation here in the South. Our immediate problem, which may put a number of areas out of business, is siltation. So, as the channel silts up, there's less water for anything, either fish or diversions for agriculture. This is kind of actual data but I’m just using an example here. So, if you have a  channel that's supposed to be 8 feet deep and the export pumps lower that one foot, the diverter the fish, they still have 7 feet of water right? If over the years the silt goes all the way up here, and now you have 2 feet deep of water, and the exports take a foot off. Now, when I first started doing this we just kind of assumed, you know, there wasn't really data that when you have high flow years, that kind of pushes the silt out. Some point we reached a tipping point, and now we just had a big high flow year last year, and everything got significantly worse. Now it’s very bad, so the short term is I have to figure out how we can re-establish the Channel depths. A dredging project which is, millions of dollars, millions of dollars in regulatory nightmare. So that's my immediate problem. The other problem is the amount of flow coming down the river, both for fish and us. The regulators have windows of elevated flows for fish and then the rest of year they don't care about other beneficial uses, and there are lots of other beneficial uses. The salinity problem that we experience is not direct ocean salinity coming in, our salinity is coming from upstream. And this gets kind of complicated. I don't want to waste too much time, but when they built the projects, the projects take water out of the Delta and it has some ocean salt in it  just from the normal tides. It's not at a high level, but depending upon how much they divert, the deliver a million tons of salt into the San Joaquin Valley, and then a lot of that makes its way back into the river at concentrations that are no good. So if you go upstream of say Merced, you get really horrible water, and then it's slowly diluted as you go down. But all the salt is still coming, so most of that salt now is, or originally was, ocean salt. But it's not like the ocean came in. It's somebody just took part little bits of it and then concentrated. So that's our big problem is that salt. Now, again, it gets complicated because the lands down there had salt in some naturally.So that salt was being drained too, but after a hundred years of irrigation the root zone of the soil,  the natural salts have been leached out. So  we have that salt problem, water level problem, flow problem. So that's our immediate worries. When you get in to and get cut me off if I'm rambling too much here. But when you get into, the future scenarios that people are predicting --That's a whole other ball game. When you ask me what's the Delta gonna look like in 30 or 50 years?

conversation.speaker: AZ
conversation.content: So the next question is, how have you been impacted by salinity in the Delta, either professionally and or personally?

conversation.speaker: JH
conversation.content: Yeah, that gets back to the differences that historically ocean salts would slowly come in in a drought. That's one of the misconceptions fomented by the State Board, which is: salt comes in and nobody can do anything. That's not how it works. When you have a drought the tides are going like this, and so the drought … slowly the tides are moving over, so the salt comes in, but it takes months for the  bad salt levels to reach the interior of the Delta. So that did happen in the past. That's one of the reasons they built the projects is to maintain salinity … prevent salinity intrusion.  So that was an issue in the past. But the South Delta, because of our location we are sort of the end of the tidal push. So, our salt problem is this weird one of the salt that originally came from the ocean exported down to the valley, concentrated, then put back in the San Joaquin River and then flows into our area in high concentrations. And the concentrations right now, aren't necessarily horrible. Sometimes they're bad, but they're not preventing people from operating, but because of the export pumps rather than the water going through the Delta channels and making its way out from the South Delta. The export pumps turn the water the wrong way. So all of those salt particles that used to slowly make their way out. They now go backwards and all get concentrated in one area. So, even though the river's not unusable  in places, because of the operation of the export pumps , now that's concentrated and it's still usable. But it's detrimental and does ruin crops. And we do see that fairly regularly in a couple aeas. So the salt issue for me is kind of related to the ocean, but it's not that problem that most people are thinking of which is:  Gee if the sea level rises salt's gonna start coming in because we don't have enough out flow.  That's a different impact that could reach us someday but that's not our problem now, or in the short term future, near term.

conversation.speaker: AZ
conversation.content: Are there any particular things or phenomena that you would like to see protected in the Delta.

conversation.speaker: JH
conversation.content: Yes! There is a line of thought that this Delta’s an unnatural situation, because we built levees, and they did dredging and that that's true. I don't know how you could undo that, and I don't think it would be better, only because if the Delta went back to a Marsh land, partial Marsh land, there was still channels, that would actually consume more water than agriculture does. So if you go back to natural situations, it's probably worse for everything.  There's less water, still fighting over how much, It sounds weird to say -- the way we change it has to be the way it stays --- because we, you know, the change wasn't really well thought out. But you have to maintain a freshwater estuary both for the fish and for people. That's the trick here. And I, I don't want to personally blame anybody on the regulatory side, but I try to not so tactfully remind them periodically, that it's under your watch that the fisheries are disappearing. Doesn’t that bother you? You know that doesn't make the solution easy, but that should bother people. That the populations have crashed on almost everything. There's like 3 Delta smelt left, literally. Nobody punished for that.  So the Delta needs to be maintained as a freshwater estuary so that you can have agriculture. There's statutes that are supposed to require that you can have agriculture, you can have municipal uses, you can have boating uses, you can have fishing uses, you can have fish themselves, all the beneficial uses  are contingent upon this freshwater estuary. I'm not saying we should stop tides or anything. But you know the that's the way it should be, because that's the ecosystem that everybody is dependent upon. And again. I don't represent fish, but you know they're destroying the fisheries right? You know. You tell the people [they say],  ‘oh, it's the fisherman in the ocean, they're killing them all’.  It  needs to be maintained as a fresh water estuary for all beneficial uses, I guess, is the succinct answer.

And the Delta, as I understand it, is one their of their supply of water.  They've done a good job at conservation, but anyway, that's one of their supplies of water, and then we have 5 million acre feet of demand, south of me, in the valley for Ag. And that’s wonderfully productive Ag. I’m not saying we shouldn’t have ag, but you've got the millions of acre feet of need in Southern California and the 5 million acre feet of need in the valley. And that water coming out of the Delta kills the fisheries and destroys the water quality. So, what's the answer to that? The answer for the past 40 years has been well, we'll kind of not really enforce the rules so that they can still get exports. And again, those exports are very beneficial to people and stuff, but they didn't enforce the rules. If they had enforced the rules then everybody would have adjusted, you know found other sources  or not done this or that, but they didn't. So, they fudged on the rules. So, we're in this situation now where each year we start out each year a few 1 million acre feet short. And then there's requirements for fisheries, which are necessary, and so that tension between- we have to get exports and the fisheries are all dying, the South Delta people are hurt every year.
